title: Regression Discontinuity Designs in Economics
research_question: Under what conditions does variation in a treatment assigned by a threshold rule on an observed running variable yield credible causal estimates of treatment effects on outcomes such as educational attainment, labor market outcomes, health, voting behavior, and program participation? How should researchers assess the validity, interpretability, and generalizability of such threshold-based causal estimates across diverse economic settings?
data_description: The paper is a methodological review and 'user guide' rather than a single empirical study, but it draws on a wide range of applied examples from the recent economics literature. To illustrate implementation, the authors use data from Lee (2008) on U.S. House of Representatives elections covering 6,558 elections during 1946–1998. The unit of observation is a congressional district-election. The key running variable is the Democratic vote share margin in the previous election (vote share of Democrats minus Republicans), with a 50% (zero-margin) threshold determining incumbency. Outcome variables include the Democratic vote share in the next election and an indicator for whether the Democrats win the next election. The review also references applications involving merit scholarships and test scores, financial aid rules, class-size caps tied to enrollment thresholds, school district boundaries, welfare and unemployment insurance eligibility, Medicaid age cutoffs, and remedial education programs.
institutional_context: Many economic and policy programs assign benefits or treatments according to administrative rules in which a continuous score must cross a known cutoff: scholarship awards based on test scores, financial aid based on need indices, class-size reductions triggered by enrollment thresholds, Medicare eligibility at age 65, disability and welfare program eligibility cutoffs, and school assignment based on geographic boundaries. The illustrative empirical setting concerns U.S. congressional elections, where the candidate receiving more than 50% of the two-party vote wins the seat and the winning party becomes the incumbent in the subsequent election. Because vote shares contain a stochastic component that candidates cannot perfectly control, narrowly decided races plausibly resemble coin flips, allowing comparisons of barely-winning and barely-losing parties. Similar threshold-based assignment mechanisms appear throughout education, labor, health, and political institutions, motivating a unified framework for interpreting causal effects identified at such cutoffs.
